**Pre-training Techniques.** The goal of pre-training techniques is to provide model training with good initializations. Recently, language model pre-training techniques such as [10, 23, 24] have shown to largely improve the performance on multiple natural language processing tasks. As the most widely used one, BERT [10] builds on the Transformer [30] architecture and improves the pre-training using a masked language model for bidirectional representation. Previously, BERT has been applied on EHR data to leverage unlabeled data for medication recommendation [27]. In this paper, we adapt the framework of BERT and pre-train our clinical trial EC embedding using large medical corpora.
**Trial EC Sentence Embedding Using BERT** Clinical trial ECs are in the form of unstructured text. To embed these data into meaningful vector representations, we use a pre-trained BERT model as the base model for word and sentence representations. Based on a multilayer Transformer encoder [30], BERT is pre-trained using two unsupervised tasks.
**Figure 1: The DeepEnroll framework. DeepEnroll applies a pre-trained BERT model to encode clinical trial information into** **sentence embedding** _U_ **. And the hierarchical embedding model encodes patient health data into embedding** _V_ **. Then the distributed** **representation** _U_ **and** _V_ **are soft-aligned to capture the interaction from each side. In addition, DeepEnroll is augmented by a numer-** **ical information embedding and entailment module to explicitly match numerical information representations (NIR) and reason over** **numerical information in EC and EHR. At last, the match module predicts the matching scores from the interaction representations** _r_ 1 **and** _r_ 2 **. The results will be further updated by the result of numerical information entailment.**
(1) Masked Language Model. Instead of predicting words based on previous words, BERT predicts randomly masked words in a sequence to learn better bidirectional representations. (2) Next Sentence Prediction. In order to gain better sentence embedding results which is used in our further matching prediction task, BERT has a binary sentence prediction task to predict whether one sentence is the next sentence of the other.

While the aforementioned studies illustrate potential for LSTMs as mechanisms worth exploring for aimbot detection, the ability to leverage LSTMs to tackle the problem of server-side detection of aimbot usage in Minecraft requires special design considerations, which we will detail in later sections. A different study [6], investigated a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) approach to aimbot detection in the popular online first-person shooter video game CS:GO, and saw strong results on their test set with 97.64% accuracy. This study hired a variety of players ranging from average to expert skill levels to collect data on game-play [6]. Collected data included the players’ positions and aiming angles, which were used to train their bidirectional Stacked Gated Recurrent Unit, which they claim had similar performance to an LSTM [6]. In this paper the authors trained an RNN on benign player aiming data, such that the trained RNN would produce an anomaly score at inference time for the input data [6]. The idea was that since the RNN was only trained on benign movements, any movements from an aimbot would provide worse RNN predictions (higher anomaly score) as it deviates from the behaviour of the benign movements [6]. One other approach to detect aimbotting and trigger-botting was explored by the authors of [11], where they used mouse positions, mouse events, and keyboard events to detect cheating behaviour via a feed-forward convolutional neural network. It is evident that by the nature of this problem being a time series, that some form of RNN was most applicable. We weighed the possible available options by consulting literature to explore approaches to similar problems. Common networks for time series data were Long Short-Term Memory and Gated Recurrent Unit networks as shown in Section 2. LSTM is a type of recurrent neural network that gives a solution to the vanishing/exploding gradient problem seen in traditional RNNs [13]. LSTM is known to be effective at capturing longterm temporal dependencies [14]. Further, they are very generalized and can handle many kinds of problems [14]. Gated Recurrent Unit networks are similar to LSTMs, however, they omit the output gate that controls the level to which its memory is exposed, and thus exposes the full state at each time step [15]. From empirical results in one study, it was not possible to determine whether LSTM or GRU was inherently a better kind of recurrent network [15]. Rather, it appeared as though the choice of which network performs better depends on the dataset [15]. Transformers were also not considered, since they are generally less suited towards time series data, especially when the series are long-term, as shown in a study where the authors compared Transformer models to LSTM models in a stock price time series task [16]. We hypothesized that an LSTM network would be best suited for the detection of aimbotting on our dataset’s features since the sequences are reasonably long and would thus benefit from the use of the output gate. To test our hypothesis we explored the use of both our own proposed LSTM network and a bidirectional GRU based network proposed in [6]. We slightly modified the model in [6] by switching the loss metric to binary cross entropy loss opposed to their use of mean squared error. This was done to support our desired binary outputs from the model. It follows therefore, that we also added a sigmoid activation on the output of the model. For the GRU based model we used all the other hyper-parameters detailed in [6], being, a 3 layer bidirectional GRU with 10% dropout, 64 hidden units per layer, and batch sizes of 64. Our proposed network architecture shown in Figure 2 consists of a four-layered LSTM block followed by a fully connected layer that connects the hidden states in the final layer of the LSTM to a single output neuron. For the first three layers of the LSTM we applied 30% dropout to help improve regularization of the network. We applied the sigmoid function to bind our output to (0, 1), effectively giving us a probability of whether the input data is an aimbot or not. The input to the network is a sequence of 35 consecutive movement samples from the player where each sample consists of 12 features, being: `yaw`, `pitch`, `delta_yaw`, `delta_pitch`, `accel_yaw`, `accel_pitch`, `target_x`, `target_y`, `target_z`, `position_x`, `position_y`, and `position_z` . During training, validation, and testing we used batch sizes of 128.

This improvement at the higher levels is notable with respect to ensuring both safety and fairness. We have previously identified that it is paramount that systems detecting behaviour for the purposes of disciplinary actions must be able to minimize miss-classifications as much as possible. Especially with respect to fairness, false positives would punish non-aimbotters unjustly, a result that would likely lead to an erosion of trust in one’s player-base. Further, any server operator who provides player support whether through live chat, email, or phone would incur increased costs as a result of players likely attempting to appeal punishments related to false positives. Thus, our high confidence level is critical, since it raises the bar to an extremely high threshold to be classified as a positive detection. Further, it is important that this high confidence level does not result in too many false-negatives, as this would allow many aimbotters to evade detection. In these respects we believe our LSTM network’s improvements over the bidirectional GRU shows the LSTM network would provide server operators with a powerful tool for combating aimbot cheating. Though we want to stress that further testing of accuracy in a live scenario should be conducted for safety reasons before using this model to make punitive decisions on real players.

We specifically turned our focus to aimbotting, which plagues first-person style games, where some form of combat and competition is involved. We identified a gap in any literature addressing the server-side detection of Minecraft aimbotting. We provided a background on aimbot detection techniques attempted by other authors in other online games. After some discussion on viable networks, we landed on the popular recurrent neural network architecture Long Short-Term Memory to provide a solution via classification on user movement time series data, hypothesizing that this network would outperform similar variants. Of particular interest was the bidirectional GRU network used in [6], where the authors saw strong performance on their specific dataset. We used the bidirectional GRU network on our dataset to provide our LSTM model a comparison to current literature. We identified that an aimbot detector would require very high confidence in its predictions in order to be considered fair and viable in real-world deployments. Our network provides noticeable improvements in accuracy at the required high confidence level, which provides both server
operators and players reassurance that the network is unlikely to falsely flag players for cheating. The LSTM outperformed the bidirectional GRU as shown in Table 2, with 98.5% accuracy at 95% confidence and 97.6% accuracy at 99% confidence. Further, we obtain better performance than other authors attempts at using an LSTM to detect aimbotting, although they used a different dataset [9, 10]. Lastly, we briefly explored the feasibility of this network being deployed in a real server scenario and concluded that this is possible as the accuracy is high enough to be considered reliable, feature data is collectible, and the network inference speed is reasonable.

The ability to catch cheaters is of interest to game server operators who want to maintain integrity and trust with their player-base. A form of cheating that is particularly problematic is the use of aiming robots (aimbots) that use client-side hacks to lock onto targets and perform maximum damage. Aimbots are common in first-person style player-vs-player type video games where they have the most potential to give the cheater a significant unfair advantage. Minecraft, for example, is a game that has a large online player base who enjoy player-vs-player combat mini-games. Hacked clients are readily available to the average player and thus there is a strong need to be able to detect this cheating behaviour on the server side. Significant consideration toward fairness must be given to any solution that attempts to detect behaviour that would result in disciplinary action. Thus, it is important to maintain very high levels of accuracy as to avoid the false flagging of players who did not cheat. Further, any system that does not detect true aimbotters with very high accuracy would undermine player trust in the system. Therefore, we propose in this paper, a neural network approach to aimbot detection using Long Short-Term Memory to classify cheaters based on their movements over time. Our network achieves very high accuracy at high confidence levels, providing a notable improvement over a Gated Recurrent Network on the same data. We believe the network at these accuracy levels could have significant practical use in real-world servers.

Though there are a wide range of exploit categories, one of particular interest is cheating through misplaced trust. This is the act of tampering on the client-side with the game code, configuration data, or both, allowing one to take advantage of the trust put in the client [2]. The gaming industry has long been at the cutting edge of technology, sometimes at the cost of proper game security. This has lead to an industry of cheaters, in particular among online video games. The ability to catch cheaters is of interest to game server operators who want to maintain integrity and trust with their player-base. A form of cheating that is particularly problematic is the use of aiming robots (aimbots) that use client-side hacks to lock onto targets and perform maximum damage. Aimbots are common in first-person style player-vs-player type video games where they have the most potential to give the cheater a significant unfair advantage. Minecraft, for example, is a game that has a large online player base who enjoy player-vs-player combat mini-games. Hacked clients are readily available to the average player and thus there is a strong need to be able to detect this cheating behaviour on the server side. Significant consideration toward fairness must be given to any solution that attempts to detect behaviour that would result in disciplinary action. Thus, it is important to maintain very high levels of accuracy as to avoid the false flagging of players who did not cheat. Further, any system that does not detect true aimbotters with very high accuracy would undermine player trust in the system. Therefore, we propose in this paper, a neural network approach to aimbot detection using Long Short-Term Memory to classify cheaters based on their movements over time. Our network achieves very high accuracy at high confidence levels, providing a notable improvement over a Gated Recurrent Network on the same data. We believe the network at these accuracy levels could have significant practical use in real-world servers.

Many players enjoy playing the game in its multiplayer mode. Multiplayer experiences come in the form of individual servers that are hosted by third-parties. Some of these servers have massive player bases. For example, Hypixel is an incredibly popular server that garners tens of thousands of unique players online per day [4]. The server hosts many player-vs-player (PvP) based competitive minigames in which different players fight eachother to win. There is a lot of skill involved in PvP combat. Players must be strategic, have fast reflexes, maintain accuracy, and perform well-timed mouse clicks. As many players compete to climb server leaderboards, this leads some to pursue in-game cheating to gain a competitive advantage. A community of cheaters has risen in the Minecraft scene, creating open source clients such as LiquidBounce [5] to provide a whole host of cheating utilities to the masses. One of the offerings of the LiquidBounce client is an aimbot that locks onto targets and simulates mouse clicks that are perfectly timed to inflict maximum damage in combat. It is clear to see that a third-party who is hosting a server would have an incentive to reduce cheating in their servers to boost player retention rates. Thus, the highly accurate detection of such aimbots is important to maintain player trust. Our paper starts with a background of different approaches to the aimbot detection problem. Next, we introduce a neural network approach to aimbot detection, utilizing Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) as the primary architecture block to identify aimbot patterns from movement data. Then taking inspiration from literature [6], we adopted their proposed Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) architecture, tailoring it to our use case, allowing us to demonstrate the benefits of LSTM on long-sequence data. We then discuss our results and compare them to the performance of similar aimbot detectors. We also investigate the viability of our model in a live setting. We conclude our paper with a summary of our present work along with a list of potential future works we identified. In summary, our paper makes the following contributions,

While the aforementioned studies illustrate potential for LSTMs as mechanisms worth exploring for aimbot detection, the ability to leverage LSTMs to tackle the problem of server-side detection of aimbot usage in Minecraft requires special design considerations, which we will detail in later sections. A different study [6], investigated a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) approach to aimbot detection in the popular online first-person shooter video game CS:GO, and saw strong results on their test set with 97.64% accuracy. This study hired a variety of players ranging from average to expert skill levels to collect data on game-play [6]. Collected data included the players’ positions and aiming angles, which were used to train their bidirectional Stacked Gated Recurrent Unit, which they claim had similar performance to an LSTM [6]. In this paper the authors trained an RNN on benign player aiming data, such that the trained RNN would produce an anomaly score at inference time for the input data [6]. The idea was that since the RNN was only trained on benign movements, any movements from an aimbot would provide worse RNN predictions (higher anomaly score) as it deviates from the behaviour of the benign movements [6]. One other approach to detect aimbotting and trigger-botting was explored by the authors of [11], where they used mouse positions, mouse events, and keyboard events to detect cheating behaviour via a feed-forward convolutional neural network. The dataset used for our study comes from Kaggle and contains two large tables of time series data [12]. One table is the raw aiming information captured from a Minecraft user who does not have an aimbot enabled and the other table is the raw aiming information from a user who does have an aimbot enabled [12]. The author of the dataset calls these the legit and cheater tables, respectively [12]. The data is sorted by groups of unique IDs that appear to correspond to different sessions, as the same unique IDs are present in both the cheater and legit tables. Within each table we have access to fifteen features. The `yaw`, `pitch`, `delta_yaw`, `delta_pitch`, `accel_yaw`, `accel_pitch` features describe the player’s camera rotations and their changes between samples. The `target_x`, `target_y`, `target_z` features indicate where the player’s camera is looking. The `position_x`, `position_y`, and `position_z` features specify the player’s coordinates. The `sensitivity` feature is the player’s camera sensitivity. The `time` feature in the milliseconds since Unix Epoch format captures when the sample was taken. Lastly, the `new_sequence` feature is set to true when a new movement sequence has started, and is false when the sample is within a sequence. In many other first-person combat games, aiming behaviour may involve more nuanced details of what may serve to characterize a player of being in suspicion of aimbotting. For example, in a first-person shooter style game, usually more damage is dealt by hitting specific regions of the opponents’ hitbox. Thus, information about what areas are being hit may be critical in determining suspicious behaviour. Where-as in Minecraft, the location of a strike within combat is not relevant in the damage calculations. Rather, combat is generally very sporadic, involving significant clicking, and rapid mouse movements to try and track the player during their movements in close quarters. It is for this reason that we believe the features used for detection, being the movement, aiming, and positional information as detailed above, is sufficient to make accurate predictions about suspicious behaviour. As within a game like Minecraft, it would be highly unlikely that a player would exhibit any kind of lock-in-like behaviour on a target given the nature of its combat system. The first step to processing this data was splitting the tables into groups by unique ID. We then sorted the samples by the `time` column to ensure all the readings were in correct chronological order. Next, we cut the dataset into individual samples. We did this by utilizing the `new_sequence` column in the dataset, splitting a new data point at each new sequence. Next, we removed the `sensitivity`, `time`, and `new_sequence` columns from the data row as we believed that these features were not significant to whether someone was aimbotting or not. The rationale for this is that the user’s sensitivity does not affect their targeting behaviour, the time is simply affected by the sampling rate, and the new sequence is purely a measure of when the user started their movement, which we already used for splitting the samples. We then appended these individual samples to our processed dataset array and the target class label being either 0 if it was a legit sample or 1 if it was a cheater sample. We believed it to be most appropriate to split on each `new sequence` since in practice this would be a similar behaviour to what we imagined a server-side implementation would do. The authors of BotScreen, an RNN based aimbot detector, noted that RNNs generally expect sequences to exist in regular intervals [6]. Thus, they normalized their data into 16ms intervals via linear interpolation of the event data [6]. We did not need to take this approach in our paper, as the sampling rate of the data was naturally very consistent. As many of the features vary in scale, we performed z-score normalization. We found in our testing that this normalization resulted in better convergence during training when compared to no normalization.
It is evident that by the nature of this problem being a time series, that some form of RNN was most applicable. We weighed the possible available options by consulting literature to explore approaches to similar problems. Common networks for time series data were Long Short-Term Memory and Gated Recurrent Unit networks as shown in Section 2. LSTM is a type of recurrent neural network that gives a solution to the vanishing/exploding gradient problem seen in traditional RNNs [13]. LSTM is known to be effective at capturing longterm temporal dependencies [14]. Further, they are very generalized and can handle many kinds of problems [14]. Gated Recurrent Unit networks are similar to LSTMs, however, they omit the output gate that controls the level to which its memory is exposed, and thus exposes the full state at each time step [15]. From empirical results in one study, it was not possible to determine whether LSTM or GRU was inherently a better kind of recurrent network [15]. Rather, it appeared as though the choice of which network performs better depends on the dataset [15]. Transformers were also not considered, since they are generally less suited towards time series data, especially when the series are long-term, as shown in a study where the authors compared Transformer models to LSTM models in a stock price time series task [16]. We hypothesized that an LSTM network would be best suited for the detection of aimbotting on our dataset’s features since the sequences are reasonably long and would thus benefit from the use of the output gate. To test our hypothesis we explored the use of both our own proposed LSTM network and a bidirectional GRU based network proposed in [6]. We slightly modified the model in [6] by switching the loss metric to binary cross entropy loss opposed to their use of mean squared error. This was done to support our desired binary outputs from the model. It follows therefore, that we also added a sigmoid activation on the output of the model. For the GRU based model we used all the other hyper-parameters detailed in [6], being, a 3 layer bidirectional GRU with 10% dropout, 64 hidden units per layer, and batch sizes of 64. Our proposed network architecture shown in Figure 2 consists of a four-layered LSTM block followed by a fully connected layer that connects the hidden states in the final layer of the LSTM to a single output neuron. For the first three layers of the LSTM we applied 30% dropout to help improve regularization of the network. We applied the sigmoid function to bind our output to (0, 1), effectively giving us a probability of whether the input data is an aimbot or not. The input to the network is a sequence of 35 consecutive movement samples from the player where each sample consists of 12 features, being: `yaw`, `pitch`, `delta_yaw`, `delta_pitch`, `accel_yaw`, `accel_pitch`, `target_x`, `target_y`, `target_z`, `position_x`, `position_y`, and `position_z` . During training, validation, and testing we used batch sizes of 128.
For both the LSTM and bidirectional GRU based models, we used the best model as determined by the highest validation set accuracy, as shown in Figure 3, for use against the test set. We see in Figure 3 that the LSTM was able to surpass and saturate at a higher accuracy than the bidirectional GRU during training when evaluated on the validation set. Both the LSTM and the bidirectional GRU managed to achieve very strong results on the held out test set. Table 2 outlines the results from the seven evaluation confidence levels. We see in this table that in the confidence levels of 0.5–0.9 the two architectures yield similar accuracies. However, at the very high confidence levels the LSTM starts to show noticeable improvements over the bidirectional GRU. We see this divergence appear at the 0.95 and 0.99 confidence level specifically. The LSTM was able to detect aimbotters with 98.5% and 97.6% accuracy at the 0.95 and 0.99 confidence levels, respectively. Meaning, for example, where the model was 99% (0.99) confident, it identified 97.6% of the aimbotters. This is _Figure 3._ The validation accuracy for each proposed architecture.
operators and players reassurance that the network is unlikely to falsely flag players for cheating. The LSTM outperformed the bidirectional GRU as shown in Table 2, with 98.5% accuracy at 95% confidence and 97.6% accuracy at 99% confidence. Further, we obtain better performance than other authors attempts at using an LSTM to detect aimbotting, although they used a different dataset [9, 10]. Lastly, we briefly explored the feasibility of this network being deployed in a real server scenario and concluded that this is possible as the accuracy is high enough to be considered reliable, feature data is collectible, and the network inference speed is reasonable.

_•_ An LSTM-based neural network capable of detecting aimbot usage in Minecraft with very high accuracy at high confidence levels, proving to be a promising solution that keeps the emphasis on fairness.
It is evident that by the nature of this problem being a time series, that some form of RNN was most applicable. We weighed the possible available options by consulting literature to explore approaches to similar problems. Common networks for time series data were Long Short-Term Memory and Gated Recurrent Unit networks as shown in Section 2. LSTM is a type of recurrent neural network that gives a solution to the vanishing/exploding gradient problem seen in traditional RNNs [13]. LSTM is known to be effective at capturing longterm temporal dependencies [14]. Further, they are very generalized and can handle many kinds of problems [14]. Gated Recurrent Unit networks are similar to LSTMs, however, they omit the output gate that controls the level to which its memory is exposed, and thus exposes the full state at each time step [15]. From empirical results in one study, it was not possible to determine whether LSTM or GRU was inherently a better kind of recurrent network [15]. Rather, it appeared as though the choice of which network performs better depends on the dataset [15]. Transformers were also not considered, since they are generally less suited towards time series data, especially when the series are long-term, as shown in a study where the authors compared Transformer models to LSTM models in a stock price time series task [16]. We hypothesized that an LSTM network would be best suited for the detection of aimbotting on our dataset’s features since the sequences are reasonably long and would thus benefit from the use of the output gate. To test our hypothesis we explored the use of both our own proposed LSTM network and a bidirectional GRU based network proposed in [6]. We slightly modified the model in [6] by switching the loss metric to binary cross entropy loss opposed to their use of mean squared error. This was done to support our desired binary outputs from the model. It follows therefore, that we also added a sigmoid activation on the output of the model. For the GRU based model we used all the other hyper-parameters detailed in [6], being, a 3 layer bidirectional GRU with 10% dropout, 64 hidden units per layer, and batch sizes of 64. Our proposed network architecture shown in Figure 2 consists of a four-layered LSTM block followed by a fully connected layer that connects the hidden states in the final layer of the LSTM to a single output neuron. For the first three layers of the LSTM we applied 30% dropout to help improve regularization of the network. We applied the sigmoid function to bind our output to (0, 1), effectively giving us a probability of whether the input data is an aimbot or not. The input to the network is a sequence of 35 consecutive movement samples from the player where each sample consists of 12 features, being: `yaw`, `pitch`, `delta_yaw`, `delta_pitch`, `accel_yaw`, `accel_pitch`, `target_x`, `target_y`, `target_z`, `position_x`, `position_y`, and `position_z` . During training, validation, and testing we used batch sizes of 128.
For both the LSTM and bidirectional GRU based models, we used the best model as determined by the highest validation set accuracy, as shown in Figure 3, for use against the test set. We see in Figure 3 that the LSTM was able to surpass and saturate at a higher accuracy than the bidirectional GRU during training when evaluated on the validation set. Both the LSTM and the bidirectional GRU managed to achieve very strong results on the held out test set. Table 2 outlines the results from the seven evaluation confidence levels. We see in this table that in the confidence levels of 0.5–0.9 the two architectures yield similar accuracies. However, at the very high confidence levels the LSTM starts to show noticeable improvements over the bidirectional GRU. We see this divergence appear at the 0.95 and 0.99 confidence level specifically. The LSTM was able to detect aimbotters with 98.5% and 97.6% accuracy at the 0.95 and 0.99 confidence levels, respectively. Meaning, for example, where the model was 99% (0.99) confident, it identified 97.6% of the aimbotters. This is _Figure 3._ The validation accuracy for each proposed architecture.
This paper explored the growing issue of online cheating and its effects on game servers. We specifically turned our focus to aimbotting, which plagues first-person style games, where some form of combat and competition is involved. We identified a gap in any literature addressing the server-side detection of Minecraft aimbotting. We provided a background on aimbot detection techniques attempted by other authors in other online games. After some discussion on viable networks, we landed on the popular recurrent neural network architecture Long Short-Term Memory to provide a solution via classification on user movement time series data, hypothesizing that this network would outperform similar variants. Of particular interest was the bidirectional GRU network used in [6], where the authors saw strong performance on their specific dataset. We used the bidirectional GRU network on our dataset to provide our LSTM model a comparison to current literature. We identified that an aimbot detector would require very high confidence in its predictions in order to be considered fair and viable in real-world deployments. Our network provides noticeable improvements in accuracy at the required high confidence level, which provides both server
operators and players reassurance that the network is unlikely to falsely flag players for cheating. The LSTM outperformed the bidirectional GRU as shown in Table 2, with 98.5% accuracy at 95% confidence and 97.6% accuracy at 99% confidence. Further, we obtain better performance than other authors attempts at using an LSTM to detect aimbotting, although they used a different dataset [9, 10]. Lastly, we briefly explored the feasibility of this network being deployed in a real server scenario and concluded that this is possible as the accuracy is high enough to be considered reliable, feature data is collectible, and the network inference speed is reasonable.

The dataset used for our study comes from Kaggle and contains two large tables of time series data [12]. The author of the dataset calls these the legit and cheater tables, respectively [12]. The data is sorted by groups of unique IDs that appear to correspond to different sessions, as the same unique IDs are present in both the cheater and legit tables. Within each table we have access to fifteen features. The `yaw`, `pitch`, `delta_yaw`, `delta_pitch`, `accel_yaw`, `accel_pitch` features describe the player’s camera rotations and their changes between samples. The `sensitivity` feature is the player’s camera sensitivity. The `time` feature in the milliseconds since Unix Epoch format captures when the sample was taken. Lastly, the `new_sequence` feature is set to true when a new movement sequence has started, and is false when the sample is within a sequence. Thus, information about what areas are being hit may be critical in determining suspicious behaviour. Where-as in Minecraft, the location of a strike within combat is not relevant in the damage calculations. Rather, combat is generally very sporadic, involving significant clicking, and rapid mouse movements to try and track the player during their movements in close quarters. It is for this reason that we believe the features used for detection, being the movement, aiming, and positional information as detailed above, is sufficient to make accurate predictions about suspicious behaviour. As within a game like Minecraft, it would be highly unlikely that a player would exhibit any kind of lock-in-like behaviour on a target given the nature of its combat system. Thus, they normalized their data into 16ms intervals via linear interpolation of the event data [6]. We did not need to take this approach in our paper, as the sampling rate of the data was naturally very consistent. As many of the features vary in scale, we performed z-score normalization. We found in our testing that this normalization resulted in better convergence during training when compared to no normalization.

It is evident that by the nature of this problem being a time series, that some form of RNN was most applicable. We weighed the possible available options by consulting literature to explore approaches to similar problems. Common networks for time series data were Long Short-Term Memory and Gated Recurrent Unit networks as shown in Section 2. LSTM is a type of recurrent neural network that gives a solution to the vanishing/exploding gradient problem seen in traditional RNNs [13]. LSTM is known to be effective at capturing longterm temporal dependencies [14]. Further, they are very generalized and can handle many kinds of problems [14]. Gated Recurrent Unit networks are similar to LSTMs, however, they omit the output gate that controls the level to which its memory is exposed, and thus exposes the full state at each time step [15]. From empirical results in one study, it was not possible to determine whether LSTM or GRU was inherently a better kind of recurrent network [15]. Rather, it appeared as though the choice of which network performs better depends on the dataset [15]. Transformers were also not considered, since they are generally less suited towards time series data, especially when the series are long-term, as shown in a study where the authors compared Transformer models to LSTM models in a stock price time series task [16]. We hypothesized that an LSTM network would be best suited for the detection of aimbotting on our dataset’s features since the sequences are reasonably long and would thus benefit from the use of the output gate. To test our hypothesis we explored the use of both our own proposed LSTM network and a bidirectional GRU based network proposed in [6]. We slightly modified the model in [6] by switching the loss metric to binary cross entropy loss opposed to their use of mean squared error. This was done to support our desired binary outputs from the model. It follows therefore, that we also added a sigmoid activation on the output of the model. For the GRU based model we used all the other hyper-parameters detailed in [6], being, a 3 layer bidirectional GRU with 10% dropout, 64 hidden units per layer, and batch sizes of 64. Our proposed network architecture shown in Figure 2 consists of a four-layered LSTM block followed by a fully connected layer that connects the hidden states in the final layer of the LSTM to a single output neuron. For the first three layers of the LSTM we applied 30% dropout to help improve regularization of the network. We applied the sigmoid function to bind our output to (0, 1), effectively giving us a probability of whether the input data is an aimbot or not. The input to the network is a sequence of 35 consecutive movement samples from the player where each sample consists of 12 features, being: `yaw`, `pitch`, `delta_yaw`, `delta_pitch`, `accel_yaw`, `accel_pitch`, `target_x`, `target_y`, `target_z`, `position_x`, `position_y`, and `position_z` . During training, validation, and testing we used batch sizes of 128.
We implemented and trained two architectures for our study. We first trained the bidirectional GRU based network as described in Section 3.2 using the hyper-parameters as discussed. No further hyper-parameter exploration was done for this model. _Table 1._ The range of hyper-parameters that we manually searched along with the parameters in our search that yielded the best results for our LSTM model.
For both the LSTM and bidirectional GRU based models, we used the best model as determined by the highest validation set accuracy, as shown in Figure 3, for use against the test set. We see in Figure 3 that the LSTM was able to surpass and saturate at a higher accuracy than the bidirectional GRU during training when evaluated on the validation set. Both the LSTM and the bidirectional GRU managed to achieve very strong results on the held out test set. Table 2 outlines the results from the seven evaluation confidence levels. We see in this table that in the confidence levels of 0.5–0.9 the two architectures yield similar accuracies. However, at the very high confidence levels the LSTM starts to show noticeable improvements over the bidirectional GRU. We see this divergence appear at the 0.95 and 0.99 confidence level specifically. The LSTM was able to detect aimbotters with 98.5% and 97.6% accuracy at the 0.95 and 0.99 confidence levels, respectively. Meaning, for example, where the model was 99% (0.99) confident, it identified 97.6% of the aimbotters. This is _Figure 3._ The validation accuracy for each proposed architecture.
Our lab computer setup used an NVIDIA GeForce 1660Ti with 6GB of VRAM, a Ryzen7 2700X Eight-Core CPU, and 47GB of DDR4 RAM. With respect to our proposed LSTM network, we were able to achieve average inference speeds of 8.04 milliseconds per sample over ten samples on the GPU where the GPU was given one warm-up sample prior to taking the average. We further achieved an average inference speed of 131.74 milliseconds per sample over ten samples on the CPU. These speeds are reasonable but problematic with respect to real-time monitoring as the server resources required to perform continual inference at these speeds on a large player base would be immense. However, the speeds are low enough to use this model periodically. We only explored a limited range of hyper-parameters for the LSTM model. We believe there may be some merit to exploring other ranges of hyper-parameters especially with respect to larger sequence lengths. Though we were unable to achieve convergence at longer sequence lengths, there may be a better set of hyper-parameters that make this feasible.

_•_ An LSTM-based neural network capable of detecting aimbot usage in Minecraft with very high accuracy at high confidence levels, proving to be a promising solution that keeps the emphasis on fairness.
For both the LSTM and bidirectional GRU based models, we used the best model as determined by the highest validation set accuracy, as shown in Figure 3, for use against the test set. We see in Figure 3 that the LSTM was able to surpass and saturate at a higher accuracy than the bidirectional GRU during training when evaluated on the validation set. Both the LSTM and the bidirectional GRU managed to achieve very strong results on the held out test set. Table 2 outlines the results from the seven evaluation confidence levels. We see in this table that in the confidence levels of 0.5–0.9 the two architectures yield similar accuracies. However, at the very high confidence levels the LSTM starts to show noticeable improvements over the bidirectional GRU. We see this divergence appear at the 0.95 and 0.99 confidence level specifically. The LSTM was able to detect aimbotters with 98.5% and 97.6% accuracy at the 0.95 and 0.99 confidence levels, respectively. This paper explored the growing issue of online cheating and its effects on game servers. We specifically turned our focus to aimbotting, which plagues first-person style games, where some form of combat and competition is involved. We identified a gap in any literature addressing the server-side detection of Minecraft aimbotting. We provided a background on aimbot detection techniques attempted by other authors in other online games. After some discussion on viable networks, we landed on the popular recurrent neural network architecture Long Short-Term Memory to provide a solution via classification on user movement time series data, hypothesizing that this network would outperform similar variants. Of particular interest was the bidirectional GRU network used in [6], where the authors saw strong performance on their specific dataset. We used the bidirectional GRU network on our dataset to provide our LSTM model a comparison to current literature. We identified that an aimbot detector would require very high confidence in its predictions in order to be considered fair and viable in real-world deployments. Our network provides noticeable improvements in accuracy at the required high confidence level, which provides both server
operators and players reassurance that the network is unlikely to falsely flag players for cheating. The LSTM outperformed the bidirectional GRU as shown in Table 2, with 98.5% accuracy at 95% confidence and 97.6% accuracy at 99% confidence. Further, we obtain better performance than other authors attempts at using an LSTM to detect aimbotting, although they used a different dataset [9, 10]. Lastly, we briefly explored the feasibility of this network being deployed in a real server scenario and concluded that this is possible as the accuracy is high enough to be considered reliable, feature data is collectible, and the network inference speed is reasonable.

[9]. Their feature set draws some parallels to the dataset we are using for our approach with respect to the positions, pitch, and yaw. The author performed ten-fold cross validation to evaluate their model, yielding test set accuracy in the range of 80-90% [9]. Another author explored the use of LSTMs to detect aimbotting, looking also at the game CS:GO [10]. This study used a relatively small amount of data, however, they still saw decent performance, at 70% accuracy [10]. The author notes however, that in order for their model to be useful it would need to be at least 90% accurate, which would require much more training data [10]. While the aforementioned studies illustrate potential for LSTMs as mechanisms worth exploring for aimbot detection, the ability to leverage LSTMs to tackle the problem of server-side detection of aimbot usage in Minecraft requires special design considerations, which we will detail in later sections. A different study [6], investigated a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) approach to aimbot detection in the popular online first-person shooter video game CS:GO, and saw strong results on their test set with 97.64% accuracy. This study hired a variety of players ranging from average to expert skill levels to collect data on game-play [6]. Collected data included the players’ positions and aiming angles, which were used to train their bidirectional Stacked Gated Recurrent Unit, which they claim had similar performance to an LSTM [6]. In this paper the authors trained an RNN on benign player aiming data, such that the trained RNN would produce an anomaly score at inference time for the input data [6]. The idea was that since the RNN was only trained on benign movements, any movements from an aimbot would provide worse RNN predictions (higher anomaly score) as it deviates from the behaviour of the benign movements [6]. One other approach to detect aimbotting and trigger-botting was explored by the authors of [11], where they used mouse positions, mouse events, and keyboard events to detect cheating behaviour via a feed-forward convolutional neural network. This paper saw strong performance with 99.2% and 98.9% accuracy for their trigger-bot and aimbot, respectively
The dataset used for our study comes from Kaggle and contains two large tables of time series data [12]. One table is the raw aiming information captured from a Minecraft user who does not have an aimbot enabled and the other table is the raw aiming information from a user who does have an aimbot enabled [12]. The author of the dataset calls these the legit and cheater tables, respectively [12]. The data is sorted by groups of unique IDs that appear to correspond to different sessions, as the same unique IDs are present in both the cheater and legit tables. Within each table we have access to fifteen features. The `yaw`, `pitch`, `delta_yaw`, `delta_pitch`, `accel_yaw`, `accel_pitch` features describe the player’s camera rotations and their changes between samples. The `target_x`, `target_y`, `target_z` features indicate where the player’s camera is looking. The `position_x`, `position_y`, and `position_z` features specify the player’s coordinates. The `sensitivity` feature is the player’s camera sensitivity. The `time` feature in the milliseconds since Unix Epoch format captures when the sample was taken. Lastly, the `new_sequence` feature is set to true when a new movement sequence has started, and is false when the sample is within a sequence. In many other first-person combat games, aiming behaviour may involve more nuanced details of what may serve to characterize a player of being in suspicion of aimbotting. For example, in a first-person shooter style game, usually more damage is dealt by hitting specific regions of the opponents’ hitbox. Thus, information about what areas are being hit may be critical in determining suspicious behaviour. Where-as in Minecraft, the location of a strike within combat is not relevant in the damage calculations. Rather, combat is generally very sporadic, involving significant clicking, and rapid mouse movements to try and track the player during their movements in close quarters. It is for this reason that we believe the features used for detection, being the movement, aiming, and positional information as detailed above, is sufficient to make accurate predictions about suspicious behaviour. As within a game like Minecraft, it would be highly unlikely that a player would exhibit any kind of lock-in-like behaviour on a target given the nature of its combat system. The first step to processing this data was splitting the tables into groups by unique ID. We then sorted the samples by the `time` column to ensure all the readings were in correct chronological order. Next, we cut the dataset into individual samples. We did this by utilizing the `new_sequence` column in the dataset, splitting a new data point at each new sequence. Next, we removed the `sensitivity`, `time`, and `new_sequence` columns from the data row as we believed that these features were not significant to whether someone was aimbotting or not. The rationale for this is that the user’s sensitivity does not affect their targeting behaviour, the time is simply affected by the sampling rate, and the new sequence is purely a measure of when the user started their movement, which we already used for splitting the samples. We then appended these individual samples to our processed dataset array and the target class label being either 0 if it was a legit sample or 1 if it was a cheater sample. We believed it to be most appropriate to split on each `new sequence` since in practice this would be a similar behaviour to what we imagined a server-side implementation would do. The authors of BotScreen, an RNN based aimbot detector, noted that RNNs generally expect sequences to exist in regular intervals [6]. Thus, they normalized their data into 16ms intervals via linear interpolation of the event data [6]. We did not need to take this approach in our paper, as the sampling rate of the data was naturally very consistent. As many of the features vary in scale, we performed z-score normalization. We found in our testing that this normalization resulted in better convergence during training when compared to no normalization.

_•_ An LSTM-based neural network capable of detecting aimbot usage in Minecraft with very high accuracy at high confidence levels, proving to be a promising solution that keeps the emphasis on fairness.
For both the LSTM and bidirectional GRU based models, we used the best model as determined by the highest validation set accuracy, as shown in Figure 3, for use against the test set. We see in Figure 3 that the LSTM was able to surpass and saturate at a higher accuracy than the bidirectional GRU during training when evaluated on the validation set. Both the LSTM and the bidirectional GRU managed to achieve very strong results on the held out test set. Table 2 outlines the results from the seven evaluation confidence levels. We see in this table that in the confidence levels of 0.5–0.9 the two architectures yield similar accuracies. However, at the very high confidence levels the LSTM starts to show noticeable improvements over the bidirectional GRU. We see this divergence appear at the 0.95 and 0.99 confidence level specifically. The LSTM was able to detect aimbotters with 98.5% and 97.6% accuracy at the 0.95 and 0.99 confidence levels, respectively. Meaning, for example, where the model was 99% (0.99) confident, it identified 97.6% of the aimbotters. This is _Figure 3._ The validation accuracy for each proposed architecture.
Our lab computer setup used an NVIDIA GeForce 1660Ti with 6GB of VRAM, a Ryzen7 2700X Eight-Core CPU, and 47GB of DDR4 RAM. With respect to our proposed LSTM network, we were able to achieve average inference speeds of 8.04 milliseconds per sample over ten samples on the GPU where the GPU was given one warm-up sample prior to taking the average. We further achieved an average inference speed of 131.74 milliseconds per sample over ten samples on the CPU. These speeds are reasonable but problematic with respect to real-time monitoring as the server resources required to perform continual inference at these speeds on a large player base would be immense. However, the speeds are low enough to use this model periodically. The author performed ten-fold cross validation to evaluate their model, yielding test set accuracy in the range of 80-90% [9]. Another author explored the use of LSTMs to detect aimbotting, looking also at the game CS:GO [10]. This study used a relatively small amount of data, however, they still saw decent performance, at 70% accuracy [10]. The author notes however, that in order for their model to be useful it would need to be at least 90% accurate, which would require much more training data [10]. While the aforementioned studies illustrate potential for LSTMs as mechanisms worth exploring for aimbot detection, the ability to leverage LSTMs to tackle the problem of server-side detection of aimbot usage in Minecraft requires special design considerations, which we will detail in later sections. A different study [6], investigated a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) approach to aimbot detection in the popular online first-person shooter video game CS:GO, and saw strong results on their test set with 97.64% accuracy. This study hired a variety of players ranging from average to expert skill levels to collect data on game-play [6]. Collected data included the players’ positions and aiming angles, which were used to train their bidirectional Stacked Gated Recurrent Unit, which they claim had similar performance to an LSTM [6]. In this paper the authors trained an RNN on benign player aiming data, such that the trained RNN would produce an anomaly score at inference time for the input data [6]. The idea was that since the RNN was only trained on benign movements, any movements from an aimbot would provide worse RNN predictions (higher anomaly score) as it deviates from the behaviour of the benign movements [6]. One other approach to detect aimbotting and trigger-botting was explored by the authors of [11], where they used mouse positions, mouse events, and keyboard events to detect cheating behaviour via a feed-forward convolutional neural network. This paper saw strong performance with 99.2% and 98.9% accuracy for their trigger-bot and aimbot, respectively
It is evident that by the nature of this problem being a time series, that some form of RNN was most applicable. We weighed the possible available options by consulting literature to explore approaches to similar problems. Common networks for time series data were Long Short-Term Memory and Gated Recurrent Unit networks as shown in Section 2. LSTM is a type of recurrent neural network that gives a solution to the vanishing/exploding gradient problem seen in traditional RNNs [13]. LSTM is known to be effective at capturing longterm temporal dependencies [14]. Further, they are very generalized and can handle many kinds of problems [14]. Gated Recurrent Unit networks are similar to LSTMs, however, they omit the output gate that controls the level to which its memory is exposed, and thus exposes the full state at each time step [15]. From empirical results in one study, it was not possible to determine whether LSTM or GRU was inherently a better kind of recurrent network [15]. Rather, it appeared as though the choice of which network performs better depends on the dataset [15]. Transformers were also not considered, since they are generally less suited towards time series data, especially when the series are long-term, as shown in a study where the authors compared Transformer models to LSTM models in a stock price time series task [16]. We hypothesized that an LSTM network would be best suited for the detection of aimbotting on our dataset’s features since the sequences are reasonably long and would thus benefit from the use of the output gate. To test our hypothesis we explored the use of both our own proposed LSTM network and a bidirectional GRU based network proposed in [6]. We slightly modified the model in [6] by switching the loss metric to binary cross entropy loss opposed to their use of mean squared error. This was done to support our desired binary outputs from the model. It follows therefore, that we also added a sigmoid activation on the output of the model. For the GRU based model we used all the other hyper-parameters detailed in [6], being, a 3 layer bidirectional GRU with 10% dropout, 64 hidden units per layer, and batch sizes of 64. Our proposed network architecture shown in Figure 2 consists of a four-layered LSTM block followed by a fully connected layer that connects the hidden states in the final layer of the LSTM to a single output neuron. For the first three layers of the LSTM we applied 30% dropout to help improve regularization of the network. We applied the sigmoid function to bind our output to (0, 1), effectively giving us a probability of whether the input data is an aimbot or not. The input to the network is a sequence of 35 consecutive movement samples from the player where each sample consists of 12 features, being: `yaw`, `pitch`, `delta_yaw`, `delta_pitch`, `accel_yaw`, `accel_pitch`, `target_x`, `target_y`, `target_z`, `position_x`, `position_y`, and `position_z` . During training, validation, and testing we used batch sizes of 128.
We implemented and trained two architectures for our study. We first trained the bidirectional GRU based network as described in Section 3.2 using the hyper-parameters as discussed. No further hyper-parameter exploration was done for this model. _Table 1._ The range of hyper-parameters that we manually searched along with the parameters in our search that yielded the best results for our LSTM model.
For both the LSTM and bidirectional GRU based models, we used the best model as determined by the highest validation set accuracy, as shown in Figure 3, for use against the test set. We see in Figure 3 that the LSTM was able to surpass and saturate at a higher accuracy than the bidirectional GRU during training when evaluated on the validation set. Both the LSTM and the bidirectional GRU managed to achieve very strong results on the held out test set. Table 2 outlines the results from the seven evaluation confidence levels. We see in this table that in the confidence levels of 0.5–0.9 the two architectures yield similar accuracies. However, at the very high confidence levels the LSTM starts to show noticeable improvements over the bidirectional GRU. We see this divergence appear at the 0.95 and 0.99 confidence level specifically. The LSTM was able to detect aimbotters with 98.5% and 97.6% accuracy at the 0.95 and 0.99 confidence levels, respectively. Meaning, for example, where the model was 99% (0.99) confident, it identified 97.6% of the aimbotters. This is _Figure 3._ The validation accuracy for each proposed architecture.
This paper explored the growing issue of online cheating and its effects on game servers. We specifically turned our focus to aimbotting, which plagues first-person style games, where some form of combat and competition is involved. We identified a gap in any literature addressing the server-side detection of Minecraft aimbotting. We provided a background on aimbot detection techniques attempted by other authors in other online games. After some discussion on viable networks, we landed on the popular recurrent neural network architecture Long Short-Term Memory to provide a solution via classification on user movement time series data, hypothesizing that this network would outperform similar variants. Of particular interest was the bidirectional GRU network used in [6], where the authors saw strong performance on their specific dataset. We used the bidirectional GRU network on our dataset to provide our LSTM model a comparison to current literature. We identified that an aimbot detector would require very high confidence in its predictions in order to be considered fair and viable in real-world deployments. As many players compete to climb server leaderboards, this leads some to pursue in-game cheating to gain a competitive advantage. A community of cheaters has risen in the Minecraft scene, creating open source clients such as LiquidBounce [5] to provide a whole host of cheating utilities to the masses. It is clear to see that a third-party who is hosting a server would have an incentive to reduce cheating in their servers to boost player retention rates. Thus, the highly accurate detection of such aimbots is important to maintain player trust. Our paper starts with a background of different approaches to the aimbot detection problem. Next, we introduce a neural network approach to aimbot detection, utilizing Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) as the primary architecture block to identify aimbot patterns from movement data. Then taking inspiration from literature [6], we adopted their proposed Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) architecture, tailoring it to our use case, allowing us to demonstrate the benefits of LSTM on long-sequence data. We then discuss our results and compare them to the performance of similar aimbot detectors. We also investigate the viability of our model in a live setting. The author performed ten-fold cross validation to evaluate their model, yielding test set accuracy in the range of 80-90% [9]. Another author explored the use of LSTMs to detect aimbotting, looking also at the game CS:GO [10]. This study used a relatively small amount of data, however, they still saw decent performance, at 70% accuracy [10]. The author notes however, that in order for their model to be useful it would need to be at least 90% accurate, which would require much more training data [10]. While the aforementioned studies illustrate potential for LSTMs as mechanisms worth exploring for aimbot detection, the ability to leverage LSTMs to tackle the problem of server-side detection of aimbot usage in Minecraft requires special design considerations, which we will detail in later sections. A different study [6], investigated a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) approach to aimbot detection in the popular online first-person shooter video game CS:GO, and saw strong results on their test set with 97.64% accuracy. This study hired a variety of players ranging from average to expert skill levels to collect data on game-play [6]. Collected data included the players’ positions and aiming angles, which were used to train their bidirectional Stacked Gated Recurrent Unit, which they claim had similar performance to an LSTM [6]. In this paper the authors trained an RNN on benign player aiming data, such that the trained RNN would produce an anomaly score at inference time for the input data [6]. The idea was that since the RNN was only trained on benign movements, any movements from an aimbot would provide worse RNN predictions (higher anomaly score) as it deviates from the behaviour of the benign movements [6]. One other approach to detect aimbotting and trigger-botting was explored by the authors of [11], where they used mouse positions, mouse events, and keyboard events to detect cheating behaviour via a feed-forward convolutional neural network. This paper saw strong performance with 99.2% and 98.9% accuracy for their trigger-bot and aimbot, respectively
It is evident that by the nature of this problem being a time series, that some form of RNN was most applicable. We weighed the possible available options by consulting literature to explore approaches to similar problems. Common networks for time series data were Long Short-Term Memory and Gated Recurrent Unit networks as shown in Section 2. LSTM is a type of recurrent neural network that gives a solution to the vanishing/exploding gradient problem seen in traditional RNNs [13]. LSTM is known to be effective at capturing longterm temporal dependencies [14]. Further, they are very generalized and can handle many kinds of problems [14]. Gated Recurrent Unit networks are similar to LSTMs, however, they omit the output gate that controls the level to which its memory is exposed, and thus exposes the full state at each time step [15]. From empirical results in one study, it was not possible to determine whether LSTM or GRU was inherently a better kind of recurrent network [15]. Rather, it appeared as though the choice of which network performs better depends on the dataset [15]. Transformers were also not considered, since they are generally less suited towards time series data, especially when the series are long-term, as shown in a study where the authors compared Transformer models to LSTM models in a stock price time series task [16]. We hypothesized that an LSTM network would be best suited for the detection of aimbotting on our dataset’s features since the sequences are reasonably long and would thus benefit from the use of the output gate. To test our hypothesis we explored the use of both our own proposed LSTM network and a bidirectional GRU based network proposed in [6]. We slightly modified the model in [6] by switching the loss metric to binary cross entropy loss opposed to their use of mean squared error. This was done to support our desired binary outputs from the model. It follows therefore, that we also added a sigmoid activation on the output of the model. For the GRU based model we used all the other hyper-parameters detailed in [6], being, a 3 layer bidirectional GRU with 10% dropout, 64 hidden units per layer, and batch sizes of 64. Our proposed network architecture shown in Figure 2 consists of a four-layered LSTM block followed by a fully connected layer that connects the hidden states in the final layer of the LSTM to a single output neuron. For the first three layers of the LSTM we applied 30% dropout to help improve regularization of the network. We applied the sigmoid function to bind our output to (0, 1), effectively giving us a probability of whether the input data is an aimbot or not. The input to the network is a sequence of 35 consecutive movement samples from the player where each sample consists of 12 features, being: `yaw`, `pitch`, `delta_yaw`, `delta_pitch`, `accel_yaw`, `accel_pitch`, `target_x`, `target_y`, `target_z`, `position_x`, `position_y`, and `position_z` . During training, validation, and testing we used batch sizes of 128.
Each model was trained for 64 epochs to match the number of epochs used in [6]. We used check-pointing during training to save each model’s weights at each epoch, keeping the weights that achieved the highest validation set accuracy for each model. For our LSTM model we performed a manual search based on intuition and empirical results. We began tuning hyper-parameters in the ranges listed in Table 1. These ranges were chosen as they were in the neighbourhood of our initial good results. We found during our search that sequence lengths less than 25 tended to result in quickly degrading performance. We believe that sequences of this length were not sufficient to capture the pattern details required for proper classification. Further, we experimented with the network size and settled on the chosen best parameters, as they seemingly gave the network enough complexity to learn the detailed patterns in the time series, while also not being too complex as to hinder learning. It may be of interest as further work to perform a more rigorous hyper-parameter search that may yield better results than ours.

The `yaw`, `pitch`, `delta_yaw`, `delta_pitch`, `accel_yaw`, `accel_pitch` features describe the player’s camera rotations and their changes between samples. The `target_x`, `target_y`, `target_z` features indicate where the player’s camera is looking. The `position_x`, `position_y`, and `position_z` features specify the player’s coordinates. The `sensitivity` feature is the player’s camera sensitivity. The `time` feature in the milliseconds since Unix Epoch format captures when the sample was taken. Lastly, the `new_sequence` feature is set to true when a new movement sequence has started, and is false when the sample is within a sequence. In many other first-person combat games, aiming behaviour may involve more nuanced details of what may serve to characterize a player of being in suspicion of aimbotting. For example, in a first-person shooter style game, usually more damage is dealt by hitting specific regions of the opponents’ hitbox. Thus, information about what areas are being hit may be critical in determining suspicious behaviour. Where-as in Minecraft, the location of a strike within combat is not relevant in the damage calculations. Rather, combat is generally very sporadic, involving significant clicking, and rapid mouse movements to try and track the player during their movements in close quarters. It is for this reason that we believe the features used for detection, being the movement, aiming, and positional information as detailed above, is sufficient to make accurate predictions about suspicious behaviour. As within a game like Minecraft, it would be highly unlikely that a player would exhibit any kind of lock-in-like behaviour on a target given the nature of its combat system. The first step to processing this data was splitting the tables into groups by unique ID. We then sorted the samples by the `time` column to ensure all the readings were in correct chronological order. Next, we cut the dataset into individual samples. We did this by utilizing the `new_sequence` column in the dataset, splitting a new data point at each new sequence. Next, we removed the `sensitivity`, `time`, and `new_sequence` columns from the data row as we believed that these features were not significant to whether someone was aimbotting or not. The rationale for this is that the user’s sensitivity does not affect their targeting behaviour, the time is simply affected by the sampling rate, and the new sequence is purely a measure of when the user started their movement, which we already used for splitting the samples. We then appended these individual samples to our processed dataset array and the target class label being either 0 if it was a legit sample or 1 if it was a cheater sample. We believed it to be most appropriate to split on each `new sequence` since in practice this would be a similar behaviour to what we imagined a server-side implementation would do. The authors of BotScreen, an RNN based aimbot detector, noted that RNNs generally expect sequences to exist in regular intervals [6]. Thus, they normalized their data into 16ms intervals via linear interpolation of the event data [6]. We did not need to take this approach in our paper, as the sampling rate of the data was naturally very consistent. As many of the features vary in scale, we performed z-score normalization. We found in our testing that this normalization resulted in better convergence during training when compared to no normalization.
compared to the bidirectional GRU which achieved 96.6% and 94.5% respectively for the same confidence levels. This improvement at the higher levels is notable with respect to ensuring both safety and fairness. We have previously identified that it is paramount that systems detecting behaviour for the purposes of disciplinary actions must be able to minimize miss-classifications as much as possible. Especially with respect to fairness, false positives would punish non-aimbotters unjustly, a result that would likely lead to an erosion of trust in one’s player-base. Further, any server operator who provides player support whether through live chat, email, or phone would incur increased costs as a result of players likely attempting to appeal punishments related to false positives. Thus, our high confidence level is critical, since it raises the bar to an extremely high threshold to be classified as a positive detection. Further, it is important that this high confidence level does not result in too many false-negatives, as this would allow many aimbotters to evade detection. In these respects we believe our LSTM network’s improvements over the bidirectional GRU shows the LSTM network would provide server operators with a powerful tool for combating aimbot cheating. Though we want to stress that further testing of accuracy in a live scenario should be conducted for safety reasons before using this model to make punitive decisions on real players.
Our lab computer setup used an NVIDIA GeForce 1660Ti with 6GB of VRAM, a Ryzen7 2700X Eight-Core CPU, and 47GB of DDR4 RAM. With respect to our proposed LSTM network, we were able to achieve average inference speeds of 8.04 milliseconds per sample over ten samples on the GPU where the GPU was given one warm-up sample prior to taking the average. We further achieved an average inference speed of 131.74 milliseconds per sample over ten samples on the CPU. These speeds are reasonable but problematic with respect to real-time monitoring as the server resources required to perform continual inference at these speeds on a large player base would be immense. However, the speeds are low enough to use this model periodically. Some recommendations of areas where this model could be applied assuming the server captures and stores periodic or rolling movement samples of the correct inference sequence length:
operators and players reassurance that the network is unlikely to falsely flag players for cheating. The LSTM outperformed the bidirectional GRU as shown in Table 2, with 98.5% accuracy at 95% confidence and 97.6% accuracy at 99% confidence. Further, we obtain better performance than other authors attempts at using an LSTM to detect aimbotting, although they used a different dataset [9, 10]. Lastly, we briefly explored the feasibility of this network being deployed in a real server scenario and concluded that this is possible as the accuracy is high enough to be considered reliable, feature data is collectible, and the network inference speed is reasonable.

Due to the popularity and economic importance of FPS games, it is imperative to shield them from cheating for the benefit of both game operators and players, especially considering that the competitive nature of FPS games provides strong incentives to cheat. Actually, cheating in FPS games is quite rampant. According to the official forum of CrossFire operated by Tencent [11], more than 80,000 players on average are banned for serious cheating per week. Moreover, anecdotal evidence indicates that the majority of cheaters are still at large. With regard to FPS games, the most common cheat is the use of automated tools to aim and shoot more accurately, also known as _aimbots_ .
Our work focuses on OP-bot, FT-bot, and AA-bot. On one hand, cheaters in FPS games rarely use FA-bot because they expect aimbots to assist but not replace themselves for playing. By contrast, FA-bot is preferred in MMORPGs since players often need to complete tedious and repeated tasks. In fact, among the most popular FPS games like CrossFire, CS-1.6, TF 2, CS:Source (CS:S), and CS:GO, we find only few instances of FA-bot for CS-1.6 and CS:S. On the other hand, a major headache players face in FPS games is that even though someone looks suspiciously like an aimbot, they cannot manually confirm with high confidence. However, when an aimbot is highly automated, it becomes significantly easier for manual detection. Moreover, FPS games are quite dynamic, interactive, and complicated. The automated software can hardly handle every scenario naturally. That is why cheaters prefer to use OP-bot in practice and actually OP-bot accounts for more than 60% real-world instances in our collected real game data.

**Measurement study.** Since aimbots are passive, a key challenge of such a measurement study is to obtain the ground truth from the field deployment. Neither manual inspection nor client-side detection can accurately or practically identify aimbots. To this end, we devise a novel and generic technique called _bait-target_ that can accurately identify modern aimbots for the measurement purpose. The design of bait-target leverages our observation that when a player kills an opponent, it will probably shoot one or more bullets, i.e., inertial shots. Thus, once a player kills an opponent, we immediately create a _human-invisible_ target high above the victim, which we call bait-target, as a trap to capture players’ inertial shots. Since honest players cannot see bait-targets, their inertial shots are usually gathered around the victim and will miss our bait-target. However, as an aimbot can catch all opponents and _certainly_ make an attempt to shoot at the bait-target, its inertial shots will likely hit the bait-target. In this way, baittarget can almost conclusively distinguish aimbots from honest players. Note that although bait-target is effective and reliable to capture current aimbots in FPS games for our measurement study, it cannot serve as a panacea detector in the long run as it is evasion-prone.
**When to spawn bait-targets?** Obviously, it does not make sense to spawn bait-targets casually. For example, if we spawn a bait-target whenever a player fires, we could falsely flag many honest players as aimbots. To address this problem, we leverage the following key observation:
**Where to place bait-targets?** The position where a baittarget is placed can also affect the accuracy. If bait-targets are placed very close to a player’s crosshair or it is placed near a real opponent, many false alarms could be raised. However, if they are placed far away from a player’s crosshair, we may miss most aimbots. We decide to place a bait-target _exactly_ _above the victim_ upon a kill event. When a player kills an opponent, we can assume that his crosshair is close to the victim and therefore honest players’ inertial shots are usually gathered around the victim. However, aimbots can _immediately_ catch next valid target, causing their inertial shots to hit the bait-target. Figure 2 illustrates the placement of a bait-target. The distance between bait-target and ground is computed in Equation 2.
**Bait-target is** _**not**_ **a long-term detector** . We do not expect bait-target to serve as a promising detector in the long run. Bait-targets per se are a form of security through obscurity and thus are evasion-prone. Once aimbots become aware of their existence, they could evade by shooting only at visible targets or switching off for second after a kill, even though this sacrifices the reliability of aimbots.
**Handling FA-bot.** In _§_ IV-B, we have mentioned that the FA-bot of CS-1.6 does not shoot at bait-targets. Even worse, there is no practical and reliable approach to identify FA-bot. A further analysis of FA-bot reveals that all of them avoid shooting at transparent targets through checking the rendering mode of an object. Based on this observation, we re-render _all_ players as opaque with a transparency mode. This ad-hoc technique is simple but quite effective to disable all FA-bot.
